payload.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd., vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar W/O Late ...
payload.court: In The High Court Of Karnataka At Bengaluru
payload.holding: The Court held that where a driving license is renewed more than 30 days after its expiry, it takes effect from the date of renewal and does not cover the interregnum period of the accident, but directed the insurance company to satisfy the award and recover the amount from the insured owner under the 'pay and recover' principle.
payload.ratio: When an application for renewal of a driving license is made more than 30 days after its expiry, the license is renewed from the date of renewal; thus, the driver does not hold a valid license on the date of an accident occurring during the lapsed period, absolving the insurer of primary liability, though a 'pay and recover' order may be issued in favour of third-party claimants.

payload.title: National Insurance Company Ltd. Thr. ... vs Smt. Meena And 4 Others
payload.court: High Court Of Judicature At Allahabad, Lucknow Bench
payload.holding: The appeal of the insurance company is dismissed, and the appeal of the claimants is partly allowed by setting aside the finding of contributory negligence, factoring in future prospects, and enhancing the total compensation to Rs. 13,74,876/- with a pay-and-recover order against the vehicle owner.
payload.ratio: Where there is consistent and unimpeached oral testimony of an eye-witness establishing the absence of negligence on the part of the deceased, a tribunal cannot record a finding of contributory negligence merely by drawing assumptions from a police sketch or site plan that does not conclusively indicate a head-on collision. Furthermore, even if the driver lacks a valid driving licence, the insurer remains liable to satisfy third-party claims subject to a right of recovery from the vehicle owner.

payload.title: New India Assurance Co., Ltd., vs Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharnakeri
payload.court: In The High Court Of Karnataka At Bengaluru
payload.holding: The Full Bench held that when a breach of policy conditions under Section 149(2) is established, the insurer remains liable to satisfy the award to the third party and is entitled to recover the amount from the insured, irrespective of whether the policy is a statutory 'Act' policy or a contractual policy.
payload.ratio: Pursuant to the mandate of Section 149(1) and (4) of the Motor Vehicles Act 1988, an insurer is bound to satisfy a third-party judgment or award as a judgment debtor and recover the amount from the insured even if a breach of policy conditions under Section 149(2) is successfully proved, unless fraud or collusion between the victim and the insured is established.

More often than not, literal interpretation of a statute or a provision of a statute results in absurdity.
Therefore, while interpreting statutory provisions, the Courts should keep in mind the objectives or
purpose for which statute has been enacted. Justice Frankfurter of U.S. Supreme Court in an article
titled as Some Reflections on the Reading of Statutes (47 Columbia Law Reports 527), observed that,
"legislation has an aim, it seeks to obviate some mischief, to supply an adequacy, to effect a change
of policy, to formulate a plan of Government. That aim, that policy is not drawn, like nitrogen, out of
the air; it is evidenced in the language of the statutes, as read in the light of other external
manifestations of purpose".

The inevitable conclusion therefore is that the decision in Swaran Singh's case (supra) has no
application to own damage cases. The effect of fake license has to be considered in the light of what
has been stated by this Court in New India Assurance Co., Shimla v. Kamla and Ors. (2001 (4) SCC
342). Once the license is a fake one the renewal cannot take away the effect of fake license. It was
observed in Kamla's case (supra) as follows:
"12. As a point of law we have no manner of doubt that a fake licence cannot get its
forgery outfit stripped off merely on account of some officer renewing the same with
or without knowing it to be forged. Section 15 of the Act only empowers any Licensing
Authority to "renew a driving licence issued under the provisions of this Act with
effect from the date of its expiry". No Licensing Authority has the power to renew a
fake licence and, therefore, a renewal if at all made cannot transform a fake licence as
genuine. Any counterfeit document showing that it contains a purported order of a
statutory authority would ever remain counterfeit albeit the fact that other persons
including some statutory authorities would have acted on the document unwittingly
on the assumption that it is genuine".
As noted above, the conceptual difference between third party right and own damage cases has to be
kept in view. Initially, the burden is on the insurer to prove that the license was a fake one.

args.answer:
## Judgments Citing *National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh* (2004) 3 SCC 297

**12 judgments** in the corpus cite *Swaran Singh*. Below is each judgment with the specific proposition it takes from the case.

---

### 1. doc_003 — *United India Insurance Co Ltd. v. Smt Parvathi Hebbar* (Karnataka HC, 2017)
**Proposition:** The Supreme Court in *Swaran Singh* held that the owner of a motor vehicle has a responsibility under Section 5 of the Act to ensure no vehicle is driven by a person who does not satisfy Sections 3 or 4. Following *Swaran Singh*, the court directed the insurer to pay the awarded sum to the claimants and then recover it from the insured under the **"pay and recover"** principle, even where the driving licence had expired and was renewed only after the accident.

---

### 2. doc_006 — *National Insurance Company Ltd. v. Smt. Meena* (Allahabad HC, 2024)
**Proposition:** Citing *Swaran Singh*, the court held that even if the driver lacks a valid driving licence, the insurer remains liable to satisfy third-party claims subject to a **right of recovery** from the vehicle owner. This was applied alongside the principle that contributory negligence cannot be inferred from a site plan alone when credible eye-witness testimony exists.

---

### 3. doc_025 — *New India Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Yallavva* (Karnataka HC, Full Bench, 2020)
**Proposition:** This is the most extensive treatment of *Swaran Singh* in the corpus. The Full Bench held that *Swaran Singh* (being a larger Bench decision) establishes a **strong, consistent principle**: even when the insurer proves a fundamental breach of policy conditions under Section 149(2), the Tribunal can direct the insurer to pay the award to the third party and recover from the insured. The court noted that subsequent Supreme Court decisions (including *Pappu v. Vinod Kumar Lamba*, *Singh Ram v. Nirmala*, and *Anu Bhanavara v. Iffco Tokio*) have consistently followed this principle. The pay-and-recover power is not confined to the Supreme Court under Article 142 — it is available to Tribunals and High Courts as well.

---

### 4. doc_026 — *National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Ellappa* (Madras HC, 2009)
**Proposition:** Citing *Swaran Singh* for the proposition that the **Tribunal has power to direct the insurance company to satisfy the decree at the first instance and then recover from the owner**. However, the court noted that this is discretionary — in some cases (e.g., *Meena Variyal*, *Anjana Shyam*) the Supreme Court did not issue pay-and-recover directions. The court applied *Swaran Singh* but held that passengers in a goods vehicle are not statutorily covered, though it still issued a pay-and-recover order considering the prolonged litigation.

---

### 5. doc_027 — *The Manager v. Chennamma* (Madras HC, 2013)
**Proposition:** The court extracted the following **four-point summary** from *Swaran Singh* as interpreted by *Laxmi Narain Dhut*:
1. *Swaran Singh* has **no application to cases other than third-party risks**.
2. Where the licence was originally fake, renewal cannot cure the inherent fatality.
3. **In case of third-party risks, the insurer has to indemnify the amount** and, if so advised, recover from the insured.
4. The concept of purposive interpretation has no application to cases relatable to Section 149.
The court applied point (3) to hold the insurer liable to pay and recover where the driver had only an LMV licence but was driving a heavy goods vehicle.

---

### 6. doc_028 — *United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Sukumarbai Suryakant Nikam* (Bombay HC, 2019)
**Proposition:** The court noted that *Swaran Singh* (followed in *Laxmi Narain Dhut* and *Shamanna*) **holds the field** for third-party claims involving licence breaches — the insurer must pay and recover. However, the court **distinguished** *Swaran Singh* on facts: the deceased was a passenger in a private vehicle used for hire/reward, not a "third party" under the Act. Since the risk was not statutorily required to be covered, the pay-and-recover principle from *Swaran Singh* did not apply, and the insurer was completely exonerated.

---

### 7. doc_029 — *United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Minor Mahesh Kanubhai* (Gujarat HC, 2014)
**Proposition:** The court held that *Swaran Singh* **has no application to cases other than third-party risks**. Where gratuitous passengers in a goods vehicle are involved, the risk is neither statutorily required to be covered nor covered under the policy. The court cited *Oriental Insurance v. Meena Variyal* which held: *"It is difficult to apply the ratio of this decision to a case not involving a third party."* Accordingly, the Tribunal had no power under Section 149(4) and (5) to direct pay-and-recover.

---

### 8. doc_030 — *Dadapeera v. Mallesh* (Karnataka HC, 2025)
**Proposition:** The court cited *Swaran Singh* but held it **inapplicable** because the claimant was travelling on the mud-guard of a tractor — a person not covered by statutory insurance under Section 147. Following the principle that *Swaran Singh* applies only to third-party risks, the court exonerated the insurer entirely and directed the owner to pay.

---

### 9. doc_031 — *National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Laxmi Narain Dhut* (Supreme Court, 2007)
**Proposition:** This is the **authoritative Supreme Court judgment interpreting the scope of *Swaran Singh***. The court held:
- *Swaran Singh* applies **exclusively to third-party risks** under Section 149.
- It has **no application to own-damage claims** or disputes between insurer and insured where no third party is involved.
- Where the licence was originally fake, renewal cannot cure the inherent fatality.
- The concept of purposive interpretation has no application to cases relatable to Section 149.

---

### 10. doc_032 — *S. Iyyapan v. United India Insurance Co. Ltd.* (Supreme Court, 2013)
**Proposition:** The Supreme Court cited *Swaran Singh* for the proposition that **a person holding a licence for a particular type of vehicle cannot be said to have no licence for driving another type of vehicle of the same category** (e.g., a car vs. a jeep, both being light motor vehicles). The court also relied on *Swaran Singh* for the principle that the insurer's liability to satisfy a decree in favour of a third party is **statutory**, and the insurer cannot avoid it merely because the driver lacked an endorsement to drive the vehicle as a commercial vehicle while holding a valid LMV licence.

---

### 11. doc_033 — *Satto v. New India Assurance Co. Ltd.* (Delhi HC, 2013)
**Proposition:** Citing *Swaran Singh*, the court held that the **liability of the insurance company to satisfy the award in the first instance is statutory**; it is bound to satisfy the award even if there is a breach of policy conditions (invalid driving licence), and is entitled to recover the amount from the driver and owner in execution of the same judgment without independent civil proceedings.

---

### 12. doc_035 — *United India Insurance Company Limited v. V. Vijayakumar* (Madras HC, 2010)
**Proposition:** The court extensively discussed *Swaran Singh* for the proposition that the **liability of the insurer is both contractual and statutory**, and that a beneficent statute must receive liberal interpretation. The court applied the pay-and-recover principle where the driver held only an LMV licence without the specific authorisation to drive a transport vehicle, directing the insurer to pay the third-party compensation first and recover from the insured.

---

## Summary of Propositions

| Proposition | Judgments |
|---|---|
| **Pay-and-recover**: Insurer must satisfy third-party award despite licence breach, then recover from insured | doc_003, doc_006, doc_025, doc_026, doc_027, doc_033, doc_035 |
| **Limited to third-party risks**: *Swaran Singh* does not apply to own-damage claims or non-third-party situations | doc_027, doc_028, doc_029, doc_030, doc_031 |
| **Statutory liability**: Insurer's liability to third parties is statutory, not merely contractual | doc_032, doc_033, doc_035 |
| **Licence interpretation**: A licence for one type of LMV covers other LMVs of the same category | doc_032 |
| **Owner's responsibility**: Owner must ensure driver satisfies licence requirements | doc_003 |
| **Discretionary**: Pay-and-recover is not automatic; depends on facts of each case | doc_026, doc_025 |
| **Fake licence**: Renewal cannot cure a fake licence | doc_027, doc_031 |

priority_arguments: Swaran Singh is binding Supreme Court authority for the proposition that in third-party claims, the insurer must satisfy the award even if there is a breach of policy conditions (licence defect), with a right to recover from the insured.
The pay-and-recover principle applies to all third-party claims — whether the breach is an expired licence, missing endorsement, wrong licence category, or no licence at all.
The insurer's liability to third parties is statutory under Section 149, not merely contractual — this cannot be contracted out of.
Subsequent Supreme Court decisions (Pappu v. Vinod Kumar Lamba, Singh Ram v. Nirmala, Anu Bhanavara v. Iffco Tokio) have consistently followed Swaran Singh.
The power to order pay-and-recover is not confined to the Supreme Court under Article 142 — it is available to Tribunals and High Courts (per Yallavva Full Bench).
strategy.compensation_range: Not applicable — this is a research question about precedent, not a quantum question.
risks: If the claim is not a 'third-party' claim (e.g., own-damage, gratuitous passenger in goods vehicle, passenger for hire in private vehicle), Swaran Singh does not apply and the insurer may be completely exonerated — per Laxmi Narain Dhut (SC) and the Gujarat/Bombay/Karnataka High Court decisions.
The pay-and-recover direction is discretionary, not automatic — the court may decline it depending on facts (per Ellappa and Yallavva).

If the licence was originally fake (not merely expired or of the wrong category), renewal cannot cure it, and the insurer may still be liable to pay and recover, but the analysis is stricter (per Laxmi Narain Dhut).

payload.holding: The tribunal held that the insurer proved a fundamental breach of policy conditions due to the driver lacking a valid driving licence, but directed the insurer to pay the compensation to the petitioner in the first instance under the 'pay and recover' principle, with liberty to recover the same from the vehicle owner.

The pay-and-recover principle applies to all third-party claims — whether the breach is an expired licence, missing endorsement, wrong licence category, or no licence at all.
The insurer's liability to third parties is statutory under Section 149, not merely contractual — this cannot be contracted out of.
Subsequent Supreme Court decisions (Pappu v. Vinod Kumar Lamba, Singh Ram v. Nirmala, Anu Bhanavara v. Iffco Tokio) have consistently followed Swaran Singh.
The power to order pay-and-recover is not confined to the Supreme Court under Article 142 — it is available to Tribunals and High Courts (per Yallavva Full Bench).
strategy.compensation_range: Not applicable — this is a research question about precedent, not a quantum question.
risks: If the claim is not a 'third-party' claim (e.g., own-damage, gratuitous passenger in goods vehicle, passenger for hire in private vehicle), Swaran Singh does not apply and the insurer may be completely exonerated — per Laxmi Narain Dhut (SC) and the Gujarat/Bombay/Karnataka High Court decisions.
The pay-and-recover direction is discretionary, not automatic — the court may decline it depending on facts (per Ellappa and Yallavva).

If the licence was originally fake (not merely expired or of the wrong category), renewal cannot cure it, and the insurer may still be liable to pay and recover, but the analysis is stricter (per Laxmi Narain Dhut).
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: Motor Accident Claims Tribunal under Section 166/163A of the MV Act — third-party claim.
